t: Tree of Coprimes - DFS with Value-Bucketed Ancestors
o: Rooted at node 0, every node wants its nearest ancestor whose value is coprime with its own (-1 if none exists). The brute idea - walk the ancestor path per node - costs O(depth) each and degenerates to O(n^2) = 10^10 operations on a chain of 10^5 nodes. The decisive observation hides in the constraints: values lie between 1 and 50, so along any root-to-node path only 50 distinct values matter. While descending, keep for each value v the deepest current-path node holding v together with its depth; then a node's answer is simply the deepest entry among values coprime with its own, found by scanning 50 buckets. Trace Example 1 (`nums = [2,3,3,2]`): entering node 2 (value 3), the path holds value 2 at depth 0 (node 0) and value 3 at depth 1 (node 1); gcd(3,2)=1 nominates node 0, matching output [-1, 0, 0, 1].
k: Only 50 possible values exist, so a root path compresses into 50 (node, depth) slots - one deepest occurrence per value.
The nearest coprime ancestor is the maximum-depth slot among values coprime with the current node's value; precompute the coprime table for 1..50 once.
Enter/exit DFS events restore each slot during backtracking, keeping the table an exact image of the current root path.
Scanning the ancestor stack per node is O(n * height) - quadratic on chains - while bucketing is O(50 * n).

a.i: DFS from the root carrying the explicit ancestor stack. For each node, walk the stack from the top downward and stop at the first ancestor whose value is coprime - that is automatically the nearest one. Simple and obviously correct, but a caterpillar graph forces O(n) scans per node for O(n^2) total work, which exceeds the limits at n = 10^5; treat it as the conceptual baseline.
s: Build adjacency lists and run a DFS from the root carrying a stack of ancestor ids.
For each node, scan the stack top-down until gcd(nums[a], nums[node]) == 1.
Push the node before recursing and pop afterwards.
a.t: O(n * h) time - h is the tree height, reaching n on chains; too slow at n = 10^5.
a.sp: O(n) space for the path stack, recursion, and adjacency.

a.i: Maintain latest[v]: the deepest node with value v on the current root path, stored with its depth. Entering a node, compute its answer by scanning the 50 candidate values and taking the deepest coprime slot; save the node's own slot, overwrite it with (node, depth); recurse; on exit, restore the saved slot. Each node costs O(50) regardless of tree shape, backtracking keeps the table faithful to the current path, and writing the node's own entry only after computing its answer correctly excludes the node from its own ancestors. Python's low recursion limit on chains motivates an explicit-stack version there.
s: Precompute cop[val][v] = (gcd(val, v) == 1) for val, v in 1..50.
Iterative DFS with enter/exit frames; on enter, record the max-depth coprime bucket as ans[node].
Push an exit frame carrying the saved bucket for nums[node], then overwrite the bucket with (node, depth).
Push child frames between the exit frame and now so children finish first.
On exit, restore the saved bucket; return all answers.
a.t: O(50 * n) time - every node inspects at most 49 candidate slots plus constant-time bucket maintenance.
a.sp: O(n) space - adjacency, explicit stack/recursion frames, and the 51-slot table.

w: Lead with the bucketing insight - whenever a path query depends only on attributes drawn from a tiny domain, bucket the path by attribute instead of storing nodes; here that collapses O(height) scans to O(50). Pitfalls: computing a node's answer before inserting its own bucket (a node is not its own ancestor), forgetting to restore buckets on backtrack (corrupting sibling subtrees), comparing depths rather than stack positions, and Python recursion depth on chains (hence the explicit stack). Follow-ups: the same query for arbitrary node pairs (binary lifting), values up to 10^9 (bucket by prime-factorization signature), or reporting the distance instead of the id.
